At the 661 responding households (response 58 percent), fieldworkers asked about alarms and then pressed the test button. A carbon monoxide alarm sounded when tested in 37 percent of households, although 61 percent said they owned one. A working smoke alarm was found in 78 percent. Households heated with solid fuel were the least likely to have a working carbon monoxide alarm."},{"title":"National housing condition survey 2019: smoke and carbon monoxide alarm module","authors":"National Housing Statistics Unit","year":2019,"venue":"National statistical release series","providerType":"report","abstract":"The 2019 national housing condition survey inspected a stratified sample of dwellings. Surveyors recorded a working smoke alarm in 88 percent of dwellings and a carbon monoxide alarm in 44 percent of dwellings with a fuel-burning appliance, without a sound test for carbon monoxide alarms. Coverage was lowest in privately rented dwellings built before 1919."},{"title":"Tenure and alarm functioning in rented rural housing: a cross-sectional study in two districts","authors":"Oyelaran-Whitt B, Castaneda-Fraser I","year":2022,"venue":"Lowmere Journal of Rural Health","doi":"10.5555/ljrh.2022.0415","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In two rural districts we visited 820 sampled homes (response 49 percent) and tested alarms with the householder present. Working carbon monoxide alarms were present in 28 percent of privately rented homes and 44 percent of owner-occupied homes (prevalence ratio 0.64). The gap was largest in homes heated with bottled gas. Landlord-supplied alarms were more often past their replacement date."},{"title":"Telephone versus door-to-door recruitment for household safety surveys: response and bias by tenure","authors":"Nakamura-Boyle T, Adeleke-Strand R","year":2020,"venue":"Survey Methods in Public Health","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared telephone and door-to-door recruitment for a household safety survey in the same sampled areas. Door-to-door recruitment reached 61 percent of sampled renters compared with 29 percent by telephone. After weighting, the telephone sample overstated the prevalence of working alarms by 9 percentage points."},{"title":"Fire service home safety visits: who asks for them and who does not","authors":"Rutherford-Nkemelu J, Soto-Lindgren A","year":2023,"venue":"Fire and Rescue Service research note series","providerType":"report","abstract":"We compared households that requested a fire service home safety visit with the census profile of the areas they lived in. Requesting households were older and more often owner-occupied. Renters made up 12 percent of visits against 27 percent of households."},{"title":"Carbon monoxide deaths in rural dwellings: a ten-year case series from coroners' records","authors":"Hughes-Mbatha E, Varela-Quinn S","year":2018,"venue":"Brightwater Public Health Reports","doi":"10.5555/bphr.2018.0041","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed coroners' records of 41 accidental carbon monoxide deaths in rural dwellings over ten years. In 33 deaths the home had no working carbon monoxide alarm, and 24 involved solid fuel or bottled gas appliances. Rented dwellings were over-represented relative to the housing stock."}]}
